lead: A shaft can pass the strength check and still be rejected. If it twists too much, gears and cams fall out of step; if it bends too much, gear teeth and bearings load on one edge; and if it spins near its lateral natural frequency, a small unbalance grows into violent whirl. So a shaft gets three more checks: torsional rigidity (angle of twist), lateral rigidity (deflection and slope) and critical speed. Machine-tool spindles, long line shafts and pump and fan rotors are often decided by these checks, not by stress.
prereq: You need: the torque and diameter from shafts under bending, torsion and axial loads, and beam deflection from strength of materials.

sections.h3: Torsional rigidity: the angle of twist

blocks.text: A torque T twists a shaft of length L through an angle θ = TL/(GJ) radians, where G is the shear modulus (about 79.3 GPa for steel) and J = πd⁴/32 is the polar second moment of area. The product GJ is the torsional rigidity. Converting to degrees for a solid shaft gives a handy design form:

blocks.where: with T in N·mm, L and d in mm and G in N/mm². The 584 is 32 × 180/π².

blocks.text: A common guide for machine-tool and other precision drives is 0.25° of twist per metre of length; line shafts are allowed more. Since θ falls as 1/d⁴, the rigidity diameter grows only as the fourth root of the load, but it is often larger than the strength diameter for long, lightly stressed shafts. A design answer finds d from strength and from rigidity and adopts the larger.

Bending deflects a shaft sideways by y and tilts it by a slope θ = dy/dx. Slope at a bearing tilts the inner ring so the rolling elements load one edge; slope at a gear moves the tooth contact to one end; deflection between gears changes backlash and centre distance. Design guides limit the slope at a rolling bearing to about 0.001 rad and the deflection at a gear to a few hundredths of a millimetre; the job specification gives the exact value.

blocks.where: for a central load W on a simply supported span L; E is Young’s modulus (200 GPa for steel) and I = πd⁴/64. For the shaft’s own weight as a uniform load w per metre, δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI).

blocks.text: A stepped shaft with several loads is solved with the beam methods of strength of materials (Macaulay brackets or the area-moment method): one moment equation, integrated twice with the correct I for each step, with y = 0 at both bearings. Because I grows as d⁴, doubling the diameter cuts the deflection to one-sixteenth.

No rotor is perfectly balanced: its centre of mass sits a small distance e from the shaft axis. Spinning at ω, the shaft bends by y, the centrifugal force m(y + e)ω² is balanced by the shaft stiffness ky, and y = e r²/(1 − r²) with r = ω/ωn and ωn = √(k/m). As r → 1 the deflection grows without limit (damping keeps it finite but large); well above it the rotor spins about its centre of mass and y tends to e. The speed where ω = ωn is the critical (whirling) speed.
For a mass on a simply supported shaft, k/m = g/δ, where δ is the static deflection under the mass:

blocks.where: with g = 9.81 m/s² and δ in metres. A 1 mm sag gives 946 rpm.

blocks.text: Dunkerley’s method combines the critical speeds found for each load alone, including the shaft’s own weight: 1/Nc² = 1/N1² + 1/N2² + … + 1/Ns². For a uniform shaft alone, the frequency is fs = 0.5615/√δs Hz, with δs the mid-span deflection under its own weight in metres. Dunkerley gives a value slightly below the true one. Rayleigh’s method uses the deflections yi under all the loads together: ωn = √(g ΣWi yi/ΣWi yi²); it gives a value slightly above the true one. Keep the running speed at least 20 to 25 % away from Nc, or pass through it quickly when starting.

examples.question: A line shaft transmits 20 kW at 300 rpm. The allowable shear stress is 40 MPa, G = 79.3 GPa, and the twist must not exceed 0.25° per metre. Find the shaft diameter.
examples.answer: d = 70 mm (rigidity needs 65.8 mm, strength only 43.3 mm). The low stress shows how much a rigidity limit can control a long shaft.

examples.question: A steel shaft of 60 mm diameter runs on bearings 1.2 m apart and carries a 25 kg rotor at mid-span. E = 200 GPa and the steel density is 7850 kg/m³. Find the critical speed from the rotor alone, then include the shaft’s own mass by Dunkerley’s method, and state a safe running speed.
steps: Safe running speed: below 0.75 × 2908 ≈ 2180 rpm, or above about 1.25 × 2908 ≈ 3630 rpm with a quick run-through.
examples.answer: The rotor alone gives 3590 rpm, but with the shaft’s own mass the critical speed is about 2908 rpm. A 2900 rpm motor speed would sit right on it; run below about 2180 rpm, or stiffen the shaft.

traps: Putting δ in millimetres into N<sub>c</sub> = (60/2π)√(g/δ) with g in m/s². The answer comes out √1000 ≈ 31.6 times too small. Convert δ to metres.
Forgetting the 60/(2π) factor: √(g/δ) is in rad/s, not rpm.
Ignoring the shaft’s own weight in Dunkerley’s sum. For a heavy shaft it can lower N<sub>c</sub> by a fifth or more, as in the worked example.
Giving only the strength diameter when a twist limit is stated. Find both and adopt the larger.
Saying the deflection falls to zero above the critical speed. It tends to the eccentricity e; the rotor then spins about its centre of mass.

quiz.q: Define critical speed and give its unit.
quiz.a: The speed at which the rotation frequency equals the shaft’s lateral natural frequency, so whirl grows to a maximum. It is given in rpm (or rad/s).

quiz.q: Write the angle of twist of a solid shaft in degrees.
quiz.a: θ = 584TL/(Gd⁴) degrees, with T in N·mm, L and d in mm, and G in N/mm².

quiz.q: Why can a shaft that passes the strength check still be rejected?
quiz.a: Strength checks only stress. A long or slender shaft may twist too much, deflect or tilt too much at gears and bearings, or have a critical speed near the running speed, so it fails on rigidity or whirl.

quiz.q: A shaft has a static deflection of 0.25 mm at its rotor. Find its critical speed.
Two loads alone give critical speeds of 2566 rpm and 3865 rpm. Find the combined critical speed by Dunkerley’s method.
Which of Rayleigh’s and Dunkerley’s methods gives the higher critical speed, and why does a designer like Dunkerley’s?
quiz.a: Rayleigh’s gives a value slightly above the true one; Dunkerley’s gives a value slightly below. Dunkerley’s errs on the safe side, so a running speed chosen clear of it is clear of the true value.

quiz.q: A fan shaft runs at 1440 rpm and its static deflection is 0.30 mm. Comment and suggest a fix.
quiz.a: N<sub>c</sub> = 9.5493 × √(9.81/3 × 10⁻⁴) = 1727 rpm. The running speed is 0.83N<sub>c</sub>, inside the 25 % band, so whirl will be severe. Raise N<sub>c</sub>: a larger diameter (δ falls as 1/d⁴), a shorter span, or a bearing nearer the fan.

beyond: Large turbomachines are checked with rotor-dynamics software that adds bearing oil-film stiffness, damping and gyroscopic effects and plots a Campbell diagram of natural frequency against speed. Standards such as API 617 set how far each mode must sit from the running range. Torsional vibration of engine and generator trains is a separate study. Search for "rotor dynamics Campbell diagram" and "Jeffcott rotor".

figure.caption: The second worked example. The rotor alone gives 3590 rpm and the shaft’s own mass 4956 rpm; Dunkerley combines them to 2908 rpm. The curve (damping ratio 0.1) shows the whirl peak there and the shaded band to keep the running speed out of; far above it the deflection tends to e.

spec.aria: Left: a shaft on two bearings sagging under a central 25 kilogram rotor, with critical speeds 3590 rpm for the rotor, 4956 rpm for the shaft and 2908 rpm combined. Right: whirl amplitude over eccentricity against speed from 0 to 6000 rpm, peaking at 2908 rpm, with a shaded band from 2180 to 3630 rpm, and tending to 1 at high speed.
